steps.notes: Gold passes (official-style combined run). Alpha formula is NOT stated in the prompt (D2). Targets: 4.330/2.5/3.75/2.165 = 5*max(norm(recvec rows)) with no-2pi recvec. max/min/axis indistinguishable here (all 4 test lattices have equal-norm reciprocal rows), but 2pi-convention variants fail.

Gold + itertools.product implementation pass; np.meshgrid default ('xy') gives same SET but different ROW ORDER and fails all 4 tests (order unspecified in prompt, test is order-sensitive np.allclose).

Gold passes. Sign convention r_j - r_i for pair (i,j) is unstated; opposite sign fails tests 2-4. Test 1 target is degenerate (empty (0,3) array, single particle) and passes trivially, but tests 2-4 constrain.

Gold passes. Docstring return spec '(npairs,)' contradicts actual h5 targets which are 2D (nelec, natoms): shapes (1,1),(4,4),(2,1),(8,4). Docstring input shape '(natoms, npairs, 1, 3)' also mislabels what tests pass: (nelec, natoms, 1, 3).

Gold and an independent all-particle implementation (electrons q=-1, inferable from docstring 'sum of ion-ion, electron-ion, and electron-electron cross terms') both pass. Gold has a latent NameError bug for nelec==0 (sets elec_elec_real, uses elec_elec_real_cross) but no test exercises it. Dangling 'using real_cij function from .' reference is cosmetic.

Gold passes. The function must multiply recvec (= inv(latvec).T, no 2pi) by 2pi internally, but the docstring only says 'reciprocal lattice vectors' - a physics-convention solver (recvec assumed to include 2pi already) produces points off by 2pi and fails. Own test is order-insensitive (are_equivalent), which is good but interacts badly with 10.7.

Gold passes, but an independent CORRECT pipeline failed: my generate_gpoints returns the identical SET of g-points in a different row order (explicitly allowed by 10.6's order-insensitive test), and 10.7's cmp_tuple_or_list/np.allclose comparison against the frozen target is order-sensitive. Confirmed: same gpoints reordered -> cmp False; gold order -> True.

Gold passes; a direct |sum_all q e^{ik.r}|^2 implementation (electrons q=-1) also passes. Order of gpoints irrelevant here (sum). Formula's |...| around S(k)S*(-k) equals |S|^2; no ambiguity in value.
Gold and independent implementation pass. Electron self term (factor*nelec) inferable from nelec parameter and formula over all N particles.

Gold passes, but ALL FOUR h5 targets are exactly 0.0 (every test system is charge-neutral). 'return 0.0' passes all tests; any sign/prefactor error also passes since the bracket is zero. Test has zero discriminating power (D8).

Gold and independent implementation pass. Targets are |E - ref| ~ 1e-5/1e-6 (ref rounding dominated); robust to nlatvec choice (erfc tail ~1e-50 beyond first shell) and FP ordering. Dangling 'from , ... from .' references are cosmetic. Signature matches **EX + gmax=200 call.

findings.evidence: Prompt: 'Write a Python function to determine the alpha value for the Ewald summation given reciprocal lattice vectors recvec of shape (3, 3). Alpha is a parameter that controls the division of the summation into real and reciprocal space components and determines the width of the Gaussian charge distribution. Multiply the result by scaling alpha_scaling (fixed to 5).' No formula for alpha is given anywhere (no problem background, step background empty). Gold: alpha = alpha_scaling * np.max(np.linalg.norm(recvec, axis=1)) on the no-2pi recvec (= inv(latvec).T) - the pyqmc heuristic alpha = 5/min interplanar spacing. Dynamic probe: max-norm, min-norm and axis=0-norm variants all pass (all 4 test lattices happen to have equal-norm reciprocal rows), but e.g. including the 2pi physics convention gives 27.2 vs target 4.3301 and fails 4/4. A competent solver cannot derive 'scaling times row-norm of the no-2pi reciprocal vectors' from the prompt; they must guess the authors' heuristic and the recvec normalization (test call recvec=inv(latvec).T is not visible to the solver).
findings.suggested_fix: State the formula in the prompt/docstring, e.g. 'alpha = alpha_scaling * max_i |b_i| where b_i are the rows of recvec, and recvec is defined as inv(latvec).T (crystallographic convention, no 2pi factor); equivalently alpha = alpha_scaling / d_min with d_min the smallest interplanar distance.'

findings.evidence: Prompt only says 'generate the tiled lattice coordinates ... from -nlatvec to nlatvec + 1. Return lattice_coords of shape ((2N+1)^3, 3)' - no row ordering is specified, yet the test 'assert np.allclose(get_lattice_coords(EX1[latvec]), target)' is order-sensitive. Dynamic probe: np.meshgrid(*space, indexing='ij'), np.mgrid and itertools.product orderings pass 4/4; the numpy DEFAULT np.meshgrid(*space) (indexing='xy') produces the identical SET of 27 points in a different row order and fails 4/4 ('xy is same SET as ij: True', allclose False). Physically the ordering is irrelevant (only sums are used downstream), so nothing disambiguates.
findings.suggested_fix: Either specify the ordering in the prompt ('rows ordered lexicographically in the integer coefficients (i,j,k), i slowest, from -nlatvec to nlatvec') or make the test order-insensitive (compare sorted rows / set equivalence as 10.6 does).

findings.evidence: Prompt/docstring: 'Return the distance vectors distances for each particle pair of shape (nparticles choose 2, 3)' - the SIGN of the displacement is never stated. Gold uses configs[j] - configs[i] for pair (i,j), i<j. Dynamic probe on EX2: r_j - r_i matches the frozen target (True); r_i - r_j fails (False). Both are legitimate readings of 'distance vector for a pair', and the downstream Ewald terms are sign-invariant (erfc(|r+nL|) with symmetric lattice sum), so the physics cannot disambiguate. Also note test 1 target is degenerate (single particle, empty (0,3) array) and passes any implementation.
findings.suggested_fix: Specify in the docstring: 'distances[p] = configs[j] - configs[i] for pair p=(i,j) with i<j, pairs ordered (0,1),(0,2),...,(n-2,n-1)'.

findings.evidence: function_header docstring: 'distances (np.ndarray): An array of shape (natoms, npairs, 1, 3) ... Returns: np.ndarray: An array of shape (npairs,)'. But the tests pass elec_ion_dist[:, :, None, :] of shape (nelec, natoms, 1, 3) and the frozen h5 targets are 2-D: shapes (1,1), (4,4), (2,1), (8,4) = (nelec, natoms). A solver literally honoring the documented return shape (npairs,) - e.g. summing erfc(alpha*r)/r over axes (0,-1) - returns shape (4,) on test 2 and FAILS (dynamically confirmed: 'literal (npairs,) shape: (4,) target shape: (4, 4) passes: False'). The step text/formula ('sum over lattice cells' only, c_ij = sum_n ...) contradicts the docstring's return-shape annotation.
findings.suggested_fix: Fix the docstring: inputs are broadcastable arrays of shape (..., ncells_or_1, 3); return has the broadcast leading shape with only the cell axis reduced, e.g. (nelec, natoms) for the test inputs. Remove the wrong '(npairs,)' and '(natoms, npairs, 1, 3)' annotations.

findings.evidence: Docstring: 'recvec (np.ndarray): A 3x3 array representing the reciprocal lattice vectors.' The harness passes np.linalg.inv(latvec).T - the crystallographic (no 2pi) convention - and the gold multiplies by 2pi internally: gpoints_all = einsum(..., recvec * 2 * np.pi). A solver using the standard physics convention (reciprocal lattice vectors b_i with a_i.b_j = 2pi delta_ij, so g-points are plain integer combinations of recvec) produces points smaller by 2pi and fails: dynamic probe 'with 2pi (gold): True / WITHOUT 2pi: False' under the test's own are_equivalent comparison. The solver never sees the test call, so the recvec normalization and the required internal 2pi factor are pure guesses.
findings.suggested_fix: State in the docstring: 'recvec = inv(latvec).T WITHOUT the 2pi factor; the returned g-points must be 2*pi*(integer row vector) @ recvec'.

findings.evidence: 10.7's test feeds generate_gpoints(...) output into select_big_weights and compares (gpoints, gweights) to the frozen target with cmp_tuple_or_list -> np.allclose, which is ORDER-SENSITIVE. But step 10.6's spec never states a point ordering and 10.6's own test deliberately uses the order-insensitive are_equivalent helper. Dynamically confirmed: an independent generate_gpoints that loops x from 0 upward (the natural reading of 'include [0 to gmax] in x direction') produces the IDENTICAL set of g-points ('same SET: True, same ORDER: False'); select_big_weights on it fails 10.7 test 1 (cmp False), while the same select_big_weights on gold-ordered gpoints passes (True). So a solver can pass 10.6 with a fully correct implementation and then be failed on a fully correct 10.7 purely because of an upstream row order that no spec pins down.
findings.suggested_fix: Make 10.7's comparison order-insensitive (e.g. compare the (gpoint, gweight) rows as a set / after lexicographic sort), or explicitly specify the g-point ordering in 10.6 AND make 10.6's test order-sensitive so the convention is pinned where it is introduced.

findings.evidence: All four frozen h5 targets for 10.10 are exactly 0.0 (every test system is charge-neutral: sum q_ion = nelec in EX1-EX4). Dynamically confirmed: a trivial 'return 0.0' passes all 4 tests (np.allclose(0.0, 0.0)). Worse, ANY implementation that gets the neutral bracket right but the prefactor wrong (sign error, missing pi, factor-2 error in -pi/(2 V alpha^2)|sum q|^2) also returns exactly 0 and passes - the test verifies nothing about the formula. (The ion-only misreading, -pi/(2Valpha^2)(sum q_ion)^2, does fail, which is the one discrimination the tests provide.)
findings.suggested_fix: Add at least one test case with a non-neutral system (e.g. drop one electron from EX2) so the target is nonzero and the prefactor/sign of E_charge is actually checked.

findings.evidence: Test case 4 of steps 10.1, 10.2, 10.3, 10.4, 10.5, 10.8, 10.9, 10.10 and 10.11 uses 'np.eye(3, 3) * L' (and '* L/2', '* L/4') but L = 4/3**0.5 is only defined inside test case 3's code. The official harness concatenates all test cases into one script in a single namespace (SciCode/eval/scripts/test_generated_code.py writes them sequentially), so leakage from test 3 makes test 4 work, and the gold passes 11/11 official-style. But the test cases are not self-contained: any harness that executes test cases in isolation (e.g. review/tools/steptest.py, or per-test re-runs for diagnosis) fails test 4 with NameError even for the gold solution (observed: 'NameError: name L is not defined', 3/4 pass on those 9 steps under steptest).
findings.suggested_fix: Prepend 'L = 4 / 3**0.5' to every test case that references L so each test case is self-contained.

overall_assessment: Gold passes all 11 steps under the official combined-namespace harness, and an independent expert implementation passes 10/11 - so the targets themselves are healthy. However, the problem leans heavily on unstated pyqmc-specific conventions: 10.1's alpha formula is simply not given (D2), 10.2/10.3/10.6 pin row-order, displacement-sign and reciprocal-2pi conventions that the prompts never state (D4, each dynamically shown to fail a plausible correct alternative), and 10.7 fails correct solutions whose 10.6 g-point ordering differs from gold's even though 10.6's own test declares ordering irrelevant (D9). 10.10's all-zero targets award a free point to trivially wrong code (D8), and 10.4's docstring return shape contradicts the frozen targets (D10). The problem is scorable but will systematically under-credit competent solvers on 10.1/10.2/10.3/10.6/10.7 and over-credit everyone on 10.10; the suggested fixes are all small prompt/test edits.
